title: Significant Role of Reconstructed Character on CuO-Derived Catalyst for Enhanced Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO2 to Multicarbon Products
abstract: Developing high efficient electrocatalysts for converting CO2 to value-added chemicals and fuels, especially multicarbon products with higher energy density, has been intensively pursued for in electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) progress. Here, mesoporous CuO nanostructures were obtained by a two-step synthetic method and used as the catalyst for CO2RR with the presence of iodine anions. At -1.0 V υs. RHE in 1.0 M KI, the total Faradaic efficiency (FE) of C2 reduction products approaches the maximum of nearly 60%. Our controlled experimental results reveal that the reconstructed small crystalline CuI nanoparticles play significant roles in promoting the selectivity towards C2 products, which was attributed to the stabilization of Cu + by I anion and exposure of abundant unsaturated coordinated sites of Cu + on the reconstructed surface. Our findings provide a new insight on the crucial role of surface reconstruction for the high FE of C2 products.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is expected to play an
important role in mitigating anthropogenic climate change, since this technology can convert CO2 into fuels with the electricity source from carbon-free energy alternatives such as wind, solar energy and so on [1]. The development of CO2RR technology greatly depends on exploring highly efficient electrocatalysts that can reduce CO2 with high Faradaic efficiency (FE) and low energy consumption. Nowadays, metallic compounds [2], transition metal oxides [3], transition-metal chalcogenides [4, 5], and carbon-based materials [6] have been extensively investigated and demonstrated to be effective in reducing CO2 into chemicals and fuels. Although some of them have shown superior catalytic in forming C1 products, e.g. formate or CO with FEs above 90% [7, 8, 9], the development of catalysts for producing high-valued C2+ chemicals (e.g., C2H4, C2H5OH, C3H7OH, etc.) with comparable FEs still requires much more efforts [10, 11]. Cu is unique among metallic catalysts in the capability of producing hydrocarbons, alcohols and other organic products [12]. However, the high overpotential and poor selectivity for C2+ products make it still challenging and far from practical use. The main reasons are closely related to the multiple proton-electron transfer steps and various intermediates [11, 12, 13] involved during the reduction process. In the meantime, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is unavoidable in aqueous solutions at more negative potentials since these C2+ reactions occur at these potentials [14]. Therefore, it is urgent to modify Cu-based materials for electrochemically converting CO2 into C2+ products with considerable FEs and low overpotentials.
Recently, tremendous efforts have been devoted to engineering the structures of
Cu-based electrodes including size and shape control [11, 15], oxidation pretreatment [16], alloying Cu with a second component [17] and so on. Among the various structures, oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu) has attracted particular attention due to the favor to C2+ compounds [18, 19]. Rapid removal of lattice-oxygen under thermal/electrochemical conditions could form under-coordinated, rough, and/or Cu + residual surfaces in OD-Cu, and thus result in enhanced CO2RR performances [20]. For instance, it has been demonstrated that the grain boundaries on OD-Cu surface can expose under-coordinated Cu atoms. High density under-coordinated Cu atoms could act as the catalytically active sites for stabilizing two-carbon intermediates and facilitating the formation of C-C products [21]. Besides, it seems that CO2RR occurs more easily than HER on the unsaturated coordination sites [22]. OD-Cu can also form a distinct rough surface that directly increases the exposure of active sites locating at edges and steps. Moreover, the rough surface helps to increase the local pH at the surface of the electrode which plays partial roles in enhancing C2+ products [23, 24]. The contribution of Cu + residuals on or near the surface of OD-Cu to the improved CO2RR performance has also been widely investigated through ex or in-situ/operando experiments [25]. Cu + can enhance the adsorption of CO2/intermediates on the catalytic surface and it is the key factor for lowering the onset potential and enhancing the selectivity towards ethylene [24, 25]. These
reconstructed characters in OD-Cu are usually strongly related to the surrounding environments, thus detailed and accurate structure-activity principles are crucial for the design of OD-Cu electrocatalysts.
Besides intrinsic structure of Cu based catalysts, external factors of the reaction
conditions, especially the cations [26, 27] or anions [28] in the electrolytes can also contribute a lot in enhancing the efficiency of CO2RR. For cations, it is realized that the sizes of cations can influence either the outer Helmholtz plane [26] or the electrostatic interactions between solvated cations and adsorbed intermediate species, thus promoting the CO2RR performance [29]. In the case of anion species, close-packed, ordered ad-layer structures consisted of adsorbed ions can be formed on the electrode surface [30]. The specifically adsorbed ions on the surface of the electrode, such as widely reported halide, can affect the electronic structure of the catalyst and promote the adsorption of the intermediates [30, 31]. In the meantime, the competitive adsorption of protons can be suppressed and simultaneously inhibit the HER. In addition, the oxidative-reductive cycles in the presence of trace halide anions may also change the surface structure of the primitive catalyst.
Given the advantages of OD-Cu structures and halide anions, OD-Cu catalysts
together with halide anions containing electrolytes have been designed for synergistically enhancing the efficiency of C2+ compounds in CO2RR [32, 33]. Cuenya and co-workers found that specific adsorption of iodine anions and the specific structure of plasma treated OD-Cu surface can synergistically facilitate the formation and stabilization of the carboxyl (*COOH) intermediate by partial charge donation from the halide ions to CO2. The catalytic performance of CO2RR for C2-3 products is enhanced and the total FE is above 60% at -1.0 V υs. RHE [32]. Peter et al. [33] found that the adsorbed I - on the surface of Cu foil can enhance the production of CH4 dramatically while slightly increase the ethylene formation rate. For single crystalline Cu(100) and Cu(111) planes, Boon Siang Yeo and co-workers [34] also investigated the effect of anions in the electrolyte including ClO4 - , Cl - , Br - and I - on the formation of C2+ reduction products. Their results showed that the FEs of C2 and C3 were both significantly enhanced.
Apart from the synthesis of materials to improve CO2RR performance,
understanding and setting up the structure-activity relationship have been also intensively pursued. Since these promoting factors always coupled to enhance the performance. Decoupling these effects is crucial and comprises the major task in present work. Herein, a mesoporous CuO material was synthesized via a two consecutive route, precipitation followed by calcination, and applied as catalyst for electrochemically reducing CO2 in electrolytes with the presence of KI. At -1.0 V υs. RHE, the FE value of C2 reduction products approaches the maximum of nearly 60%. Based on a series of controlled experiments, the roles of reconstruction structure, Cu + and I - for promoting the FEs towards multicarbon products in CO2RR were investigated respectively. Furthermore, the oxidative-reductive cycles in the presence of trace amounts of halide anions may induce the formation of special surface structure [35] or help to stabilize the oxidized state of biphasic Cu2O-Cu [36, 37] in the starting catalysts during the CO2RR process. The in situ evolution usually undergo
different dissolution-redeposition process to have a reconstructed surface originated from the different types of electrolyte and various precursors. The reconstructed catalyst tend to expose distinct active sites which favor the high selectivity of C2 products.
In our halides related experiments, the same tendency result is obtained that the
HER is significantly suppressed with the presence of iodine ions or bromide ions. These results are consistent with the previous studies. Cu + and iodine ions might play synergistically with the reconstructed nanoparticles for producing C2 products in the CO2RR. When I - induce significant nanostructuring of the oxidized Cu surface, the unsaturated coordinated sites may act as active sites and the Cu + and iodine ions can function synergistically enhancing the efficiency of C2+ compounds further in CO2RR. Due to the complicated coupling factors such as the pre-treated methods, the types of the electrolytes, the various reduction process, numerous work should be done to explore the mechanism.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials
Proton exchange membrane (Nafion 117, Hesen Shanghai Co., Ltd.), Nafion
solution (5 wt% in 1-propanol and water, Alfa-Aesar Co., Ltd.), deuterated water
(D2O, 99.99%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), Cu(NO3)2 ( ≥ 99%,
Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.), NaOH (≥99%, Sinopharm Chemical
Reagent Co., Ltd.), ethanol, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.99%, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.), KHCO3 (99.0%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), KI (99.0%, Kemiou Co., Ltd.) and KBr (99.0%, Fuchen Co., Ltd.) were used as received. High purity CO2 (99.999%) gas was provided by Huanyu Co., Ltd. Carbon paper was obtained from Toray. Ultrapure water with a resistance of 18.2 MΩ·cm was prepared from a water purification system (ULUPURE Co., Ltd.) using reverse osmosis process and used throughout the experiments.
2.2. Synthesis of mesoporous CuO catalyst
Firstly, 1.0 mmol Cu(NO3)2 was dissolved in 10.0 mL ethanol and then 10.0 mL
1 M NaOH aqueous solution was added into the Cu(NO3)2 solution. The mixture was kept stirring at room temperature for two hours. Then, the as-prepared Cu(OH)2 precipitates were washed with water for three times and then transferred to an electronic oven maintained at 80 °C for 6 h to make it dry. Finally, black CuO powder was obtained by annealing the powder above in air at 500 °C for 2 h with a heating rate of 2 °C/min.
2.3. Synthesis of CuI catalyst
15.0 mL 0.5 M CuSO4 and 0.5 M KI aqueous solutions were prepared,
respectively. Then the KI solution was dropped into the CuSO4 solution with a speed of one drop per second. After finishing dropping, the mixed solution was stirred for an extra 5 minutes. The precipitate was washed with ethanol and ultrapure water for three times and then dried at 50 °C for 3 h. Finally, white CuI powder was obtained.
2.4. Fabrication of electrocatalyst electrode
15 mg of catalyst was dispersed in the mixture of 200 μL H2O, 100 μL ethanol
and 20 μL 5% Nafion solution to form a homogeneous catalyst ink. After ultrasonication for 30 minutes, 30 μL of the dispersed solution was then uniformly spread on carbon paper of 1.0×1.0 cm in area. The carbon paper was rinsed with isopropanol and ultrapure water for three times then annealed at 500 °C for 2 h in air before use.
2.5. Materials characterizations
The morphology and microstructure were characterized by SEM (FEI Nanosem
430) and high-resolution TEM (FEI Talos F200X field-emission TEM). Diffraction data was collected with a Rigaku D/ Max III diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation). In addition, the N2 adsorption-desorption was carried out at 77 K (Quanta chrome iQ-MP gas adsorption analyzer). The electrochemical measurements were performed in a three-electrode system on an electrochemical workstation of CHI760E (Shanghai Chenhua).
2.6. Electrochemical measurements
The CO2RR test was conducted using a custom-made H-type cell with two
compartments separated by a Nafion proton exchange membrane at ambient temperature and pressure. Each compartment contains 45.0 mL electrolyte with 20.0 mL free headspace. The electrochemical measurements were carried out with a CHI760E workstation (Shanghai Chenhua). Carbon paper cast with catalyst ink served as the working electrode directly. A Pt plate (2.0×2.0 cm) and Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl solution were used as counter and reference electrodes, respectively. The as-prepared catalysts were electroreduced in CO2-saturated aqueous solutions via 5 cycles of cyclic voltammograms from -0.4 to -1.8 V υs. Ag/AgCl before the test. The testing potential can be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) according to the following formula:
ERHE=EAg/AgCl+EAg/AgCl θ +0.059*pH
All the data was not iR-compensated in our work. The catholytes were 0.2 M, 0.5
M, 1.0 M KI, 0.5 M KHCO3 and the anolytes were the same concentration and volume KHCO3 aqueous solutions with catholytes. The electrolyte was saturated by bubbling CO2 at a flow rate of 20 mL/min for 30 minutes before tests. The catholyte was kept being stirred with a magnetic stirrer during the test.
Gas products were analyzed on an online gas chromatograph (GC7900, Tianmei
Co., Ltd.) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector using Ar as a carrier gas for H2, CO analysis and a flame ionization detector for CH4, C2H4, and C2H6 analysis. The gas chromatograph was calibrated with standard gases (containing H2 4.8%, CO2 33.8%, CO 0.97%, C2H4 0.5%, C2H6 0.52%, CH4 0.53%, C2H2 0.5%, Ar 58.38%). Liquid products were collected from the cathode chambers after electrolysis and quantified by Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Bruker 400 MHz) spectroscopy. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was added as the internal calibration. 500 µL electrolyte was collected from catholyte at the end of electrolysis and then mixed with 100 µL internal standard solution (dimethyl sulfoxide aqueous solution with a volume concentration of 0.03%). At last, 100 µL D2O was added. The 1D 1 H spectrum was measured with water suppression using a presaturation method.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
3.1. Material characterizations and analysis
Here, a facile and scalable method was used to synthesize Cu(OH)2 nanoribbons
by simply mixing NaOH aqueous solution with CuSO4 aqueous solution and stirred the solution for 2 hours. The as-prepared Cu(OH)2 nanoribbons were eventually dehydrated and transferred into CuO with mesoporous nanostructures after annealing in static air.
Figure 1. SEM and TEM images of Cu(OH)2 nanoribbons (a, b); SEM images (c); carbon paper coated with (d); XRD pattern (e); nitrogen adsorption-desorption (f) of nanocrystalline CuO catalyst obtained upon annealing Cu(OH)2 nanoribbons.
The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image in Fig. 1a reveals the
nanoribbon morphology of the primitive Cu(OH)2. Fig. 1b shows the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image of the Cu(OH)2 nanoribbons with a width of ~50 nm and length of ~500 nm. After being converted into CuO product upon annealing (Fig. 1c), the structure of the nanoribbons vanishes and a continuous structure connected with small nanoparticles (~100 nm) can be observed. Fig. 1d shows that the CuO catalyst can be uniformly coated on carbon paper for CO2RR test. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern confirms the formation of CuO phase (Fig. 1e, PDF# 48-1548). An H3-type hysteresis loop of a typical type IV isotherm could be observed in the N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms (Fig. 1f), revealing that the catalyst is mesoporous. Its specific surface area, calculated by Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET), is about 77.57 m 2 /g. The pore size distribution, given by the Barett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) method (Fig. S1), is in the range of 10~50 nm.
3.2. Electrochemical performance
Figure 2. FEs of HCOOH (a); CO (b); C2H4 (d); EtOH (e) as well as the total FEs of C1 products (c) and C2 products (f) on CuO catalysts as a function of the applied potential in different CO2-saturated electrolytes.
It was reported that even trace amount of halide anions in the electrolyte can
exert a profound effect on the activity of Cu-based catalyst for CO2RR [36, 38]. The electrochemical CO2RR performance of the mesoporous CuO was first evaluated in CO2-saturated KI solutions with different concentrations in a custom made gas-tight H-cell. For comparison, the CO2RR performance in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 was also measured under identical conditions. The experimental results are presented in Fig. 2a-f. Similar to previous reports, C1 products including HCOOH and CO were preferred to be yielded at lower overpotentials, e.g. -0.7 and -0.8 V (υs. RHE, all potentials reported here are with respect to the RHE), as shown in Fig. 2a and 2b. Such preference was changed to C2 products when the over potential was more negative for all CO2RR systems with different concentrations of KI. Generally, at negative potentials from -0.7 to -1.2 V, the catalytic activity towards HCOOH is slightly favored in the three concentrations of KI electrolytes as shown in Fig. 2a. Only one exception occurred at -0.9 V in KHCO3 electrolyte where the FE of HCOOH is highest among the four cases. As for CO, C2H4 and EtOH products, significantly improved FEs in KI electrolytes could be observed in a wide potential range. At -0.8 V, the selectivity towards CO reaches the peak in all three concentrations of KI electrolytes and a highest value of 27% was obtained in 1.0 M KI (Fig. 2b). For C2H4, as one of the C2 products, its maximal FEethylene in 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 M KI electrolytes are 27.5%, 27.5% and 33.6% achieved at potentials of -1.1 V, -1.0 V, -1.0 V accordingly (Fig. 2d). Besides C2H4, ethanol was also produced with pretty high FEs. From Fig. 2e, it can be observed that peak ethanol FEs of 20% at -1.0 V for both 0.2 and 0.5 M KI electrolytes and 25.6% at -0.9 V for 1.0 M KI were attained. It is also found that the peak potential for FEethanol in 1.0 M KI (-0.9 V) is positive than those (-1.0 V) in 0.2 and 0.5 M KI (Fig. 2e). These observations indicate
that both the applied potentials and the concentration of KI electrolyte play pivotal roles in forming C2 products. The total FEs of C1 (FEHCOOH + FECO) and C2 products (FEethylene + FEethanol) obtained at each potential for the four cases are plotted in Fig. 2c and 2f, respectively. For all three systems with the presence of KI, their highest FEs of C1 and C2 products were achieved at -0.8 and -1.0 V, respectively. In addition, for C2 products at -1.0 V, the FE value increases from 47.4% to 54.5% and 57%, along with the increase of the concentration of KI from 0.2 to 0.5 and 1.0 M. At higher potentials of -1.1 and -1.2 V, it is found that the catalyst performances for producing C2 compounds in 0.5 M and 1.0 M KI are less than that in 0.2 M KI.
It is also noticed that the total current density is enhanced with the increased
concentration of KI electrolytes (Fig. S1a). In 1.0 M KI electrolyte, a highest value of 12.5 mA cm -2 could be attained at -0.9 V. Even though, the total current densities with the presence of three concentrations of KI are less than that in KHCO3 electrolyte at -0.9 V. This could be due to the suppression of HER when I - was introduced in the electro-catalytic processes. It is well known that the halide anions have specific adsorption on the surface of the catalyst, thus can prohibit the adsorption of protons and significantly reduce the FE of H2 [34]. When the applied potential moves to more negative side, the total current density in 1.0 M KI electrolyte also increases as shown in Fig. S1b. Therefore, electrolyte and applied potential exert simultaneously influence on the activity of the prepared catalyst for CO2RR. Besides increased catalytic activity, the mesoporous CuO catalyst also exhibits relatively high stability in 1.0 M KI electrolyte up to 7 hours. Further increase of current density in this system could be attributed to the accompanied HER originated from the dissolution or coalescence of reconstructed small particles as will be discussed later. 3.3. Discussion
Figure 3. TEM images (a, b); HRTEM images of the original part (position 1) and the reconstructed part (position 2) of the catalyst (c, d); elemental mappings (e) and XRD pattern (the inset shows the enlarged part between 25° and 55°) (f) of the CuO catalyst after reaction at -0.9 V in 1.0 M KI for 1 h.
Based on the observed enhancement of FEs for C2 products in KI electrolytes,
the catalyst after reaction at -0.9 V in 1.0 M KI for 1 h was characterized to gain insight into the structure dependent performance. From TEM image in Fig. 3a, it can be clearly seen that a surface reconstruction of the catalyst occurred after the reaction. It seems that the in situ electrochemical reaction leads to the reconstruction and part of them evolved into nanoparticles with a size of 5~10 nm (Fig. 3b). The morphological evolution may be induced by a combination of dissolution-redeposition process and particle coalescence [38]. Fig. 3c (position 1) and 3d (position 2) show the lattice fringes of 0.21 nm and 0.25 nm corresponding to CuI (220) and Cu2+1O (111) planes of the catalyst, respectively. The elemental mappings in Fig. 2e indicates the uniform distribution of element Cu, O, I in the catalyst. XRD pattern in Fig. 3f, including the enlarged spectrum reveals that the catalyst is composed of Cu (PDF# 85-1326), CuI (PDF# 06-0246) and Cu2+1O (PDF# 05-0667). The background peaks are the characteristic peaks of carbon paper as shown in Fig. S2a.
Figure 4. TEM, HRTEM images and XRD patterns of CuO-derived catalyst after reaction at -0.9 V in 0.2 M (a, b, g); 0.5 M (c, d, h) KI and 0.5 M KHCO3 (e, f, i) for 1 h.
The reconstruction also occurred in electrolyte with the presence of 0.2 and 0.5
M KI but not in 0.5 M KHCO3 at -0.9 V for 1 h. Fig. 4a and 4c reveal that the reconstructed nanoparticles are 5~10 nm in diameter, similar to those in Fig. 3c. However, these nanoparticles are amorphous in nature since no lattice fringe is discernible under HRTEM observation (not shown). For the primitive particles, lattice spacing of 0.3 and 0.25 nm could be observed in the HRTEM image (Fig. 4b) and assigned to the (110) and (111) planes of Cu2+1O in the catalyst after reaction in 0.2 M KI electrolyte. In electrolyte with 0.5 M KI (Fig. 4d), lattice fringes of Cu (111) and Cu2+1O (200) planes were easily probed also from the primitive catalyst after reaction while reconstructed particles remain amorphous. Although no fringes of Cu in Fig. 4b or CuI in Fig. 4d could be found, diffraction peaks of Cu, CuI and Cu2+1O with altered intensities can still be detected in XRD patterns of the catalysts after being used in these two electrolytes. Again, Cu, O, I elements are uniformly distributed in the elemental mappings (Fig. S4). Since the C2 selectivity in 1.0 M KI electrolyte is the best among the three different concentration of KI electrolytes, the amorphous reconstructed nanoparticles in 0.2 and 0.5 M KI electrolytes seems less active than their reconstructed crystalline counterpart in 1.0 M KI electrolyte. Without the presence of KI, no small particles derived from reconstruction for the catalyst in KHCO3 electrolyte (Fig. 4e). Definitely, there is no fringe or peaks of CuI in the HRTEM image or in the corresponding XRD pattern (Fig. 4f and 4i). The electrochemically active surface areas (ECSA) of the catalysts after reactions in the electrolytes with 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 M KI for 1 h at -0.9 V were determined by measuring the double layer capacitances in 0.1 M KHCO3 (Fig. S3) [40] and used for calculating surface roughness factors. The values of surface roughness factors are 274, 129 and 74.1 for catalysts reacted in the electrolytes with 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 M KI using the polycrystalline Cu foil as the reference (Fig. S3). Apparently, the FEs of C2 products are not in linear with their relative surface roughness in our systems. To decouple the effects among the factors including the presence of halide anion as well as the reconstruction and roughness of the catalyst on the CO2RR performance, three different controlled experiments were carried out.
Figure 5. FEs and products distribution (a); XRD pattern (b) of the reconstructed CuO-derived catalyst after being further used as catalyst for CO2RR in 0.5 M KHCO3 at -0.9 V for 1 h.
In the first case, the surface reconstruction of the catalyst was firstly achieved via
conducting the CO2RR at -0.9 V in 1.0 M KI for 1 h and then the performance of the catalyst was further tested in 0.5 M KHCO3 at -0.9 V for another 1 h. By changing from 1.0 M KI to 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte at -0.9 V, the FE of C1 products was slightly increased from 24% to 34% while the FE of C2 products was dramatically decreased from 42% to 7% (Fig. 2c and 2f as well as Fig. 5a). Compared with the results obtained in KHCO3 (Fig. 2c and 2f), the FEs of C1 and C2 products in the second running process are both enhanced from 16% and 5% to 34% and 7%, respectively (Fig. 5a). Additionally, unlike before second running (Fig. 3f), peaks of CuI in XRD pattern disappear after second running in 0.5 M KHCO3 at -0.9 V (Fig. 5b). Such disappearance might be due to the dissolution of CuI into the electrolyte in the second running process and causes the content of CuI in the catalyst to decrease down to below the detection limit of XRD characterization. Since the amount of I - in the second running process, mainly derived from CuI formed in the reconstruction process, is far less than those in three electrolytes with the addition of KI, a higher selectivity of C1 over C2 products was observed. This follows the trend derived from calculating the FE ratio of C1/C2 in Fig. 2c and 2f. Due to the decrease of I - , the suppression of HER is less effective.
were prepared via a direct precipitation from CuSO4 and KI aqueous solutions and then used as catalyst for CO2RR in 1.0 M KI at -0.9 V for 1 h (Fig. S2b). In comparison with the FEs in Fig. 2, the total FE of C1 and C2 products is similar to those using mesoporous CuO catalyst in electrolytes with three different concentration of KI. The nearly ~70% FE consists of ~61% C1 species and ~9% ethylene C2 product (Fig. 6a). After reaction, XRD pattern (Fig. 6b) reveals that three phases of Cu2+1O, CuI and Cu, similar to the results of the CuO conducted in KI electrolytes, could be also indexed with different contents as manifested from their variation of peak intensities. Therefore, a dissolution of CuI and subsequent conversion to Cu2+1O and reduction to Cu would take place during the CO2RR process. The elemental mappings in Fig. S5 also verify the uniform element distributions of Cu, O, I elements in the catalyst after reaction. The dramatic decrease of C2 products, especially no detectable ethanol could be detected in this case, suggests that the microstrucutre of the nanocrystalline CuI does not favor the production of C2 products. It is expected that
the above dissolution-redeposition process between the Cu2+1O and the CuI on the interface of the nanocrystalline CuI catalyst (Fig. 6c), but may not produce large amounts of small CuI particles with several nanometer dimensional size like those in Fig.3 and 4. After CO2RR, there are no small nanoparticles around the catalyst, implying that no obvious surface reconstruction occurred.
XRD pattern (b, c) of CuO catalyst in 0.5 M KBr at -0.9 V for 1 h of CO2 electroreduction.
Finally, the performance of CO2RR on the mesoporous CuO catalyst in 0.5 M
KBr electrolyte was also investigated. HCOOH is the main C1 product while the production of CO is negligible. The FE of HCOOH can reach a maximum of ~55% at -0.9 V (as shown in Fig. 7a). Apparently, the production of C2 products are quite low in the whole potential range of -0.7 to -1.2 V as the remaining FEs, after subtracting FEs of HER and HCOOH, is less than 10% (Fig. 7a). From the TEM image in Fig. 7b, reconstructured small nanoparticles akin to those observed in KI systems were barely observable. Again, Cu and Cu2+1O phases are presented on the electrode after reaction (XRD patterns in Fig. 7c). The absence of CuBr here is believed to be due to its higher solubility than CuI in water. The poor FE for C2 products could be attributed to the absence of either reconstructed CuBr or small CuI particles. Thus, the reconstructed character is crucial in producing C2 products
During the CO2RR, the mesoporous CuO catalyst could be converted into Cu,
Cu2+1O and CuI via the dynamic evolution of dissolution-redeposition process between Cu + and I - as a result of small solubility of CuI in KI electrolyte. For our mesoporous CuO catalyst, its FE of C2 products in KI electrolytes can be improved sufficiently by optimizing its local environment including the particle size, crystallinity and amount of CuI during the reconstruction process. From all above experimental results, the involved factors promoting the formation of C2 products in our system could be decoupled with their specific contributions as following: (1) The high surface area and mesoporous nature of CuO facilitates its surface reconstruction. (2) The presence of I - in the reaction system helps to stabilize Cu + and suppress the H2 production. (3) Small CuI nanoparticles with 5~10 nm diameter derived from surface reconstruction have abundant unsaturated coordination sites that can facilitate the adsorption of the intermediates for further reduction and promote C-C formation [21]. (4) Crystalline CuI nanoparticles could be obtained in higher concentration of KI in the electrolyte. The higher crystallinity and more amount of small CuI nanoparticles formed in the reconstruction process are conducive for enhancing the production of C2 products.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, a facile method was developed to produce a highly efficient CuO
mesoporous material, which exhibits enhanced electro-catalytic activities toward the CO2RR using KI electrolytes. At -1.0 V, the FE towards C2 reduction products (C2H4 and EtOH) reaches ~60% in the presence of 1.0 M KI aqueous solution. It was found that the CuO mesoporous materials underwent a surficial reconstruction and evolve into small CuI nanoparticles with their particle size in the range of 5-10 nm during electrocatalytic process in KI electrolytes. However, the crystallinity of the resultant CuI nanoparticles has a close relation with the concentration of KI in the electrolyte and could be improved with the increase of the concentration of KI. By analyzing the correlations of the catalytic performances and the evolution of surface morphology as well as the compositions of the catalyst in different electrolytes, it can be deduced that that the reconstructed small crystalline CuI nanoparticles are crucial for boosting the catalytic performance for C2+ products. Besides suppressing HER, I - helps to induce surface reconstructions of the copper oxides and stabilize Cu +
in. the catalyst. The
unsaturated coordinated sites on the surface of small CuI nanoparticles resulted from surficial reconstruction may act as active sites for the adsorption of intermediates and function synergistically with I - to enhance the efficiency of C2 compounds further in
